title: Introduce visual RAG flow designer + TypeScript SDK examples for tool-calling prototypes
author: Eleanor Chen
release_notes: Added a browser-based visual RAG flow designer quickstart + TypeScript SDK sample demonstrating tool-calling patterns; docs and images included.
description:
Context and motivation: This PR adds a lightweight, browser-first visual RAG flow designer aimed at product and developer teams who want to prototype retrieval-augmented generation pipelines and tool-calling interactions without spinning up a backend. The goal is to lower the barrier for experimentation: users can wire up a retriever, sketch prompt templates, attach simple tool stubs, and run end-to-end examples using a local LLM shim or Redwood hosted endpoints.

What this delivers: a new examples workspace (examples/visual-rag-workbench) with a React-based flow canvas, a minimal local shim (node) that emulates token streaming and function/tool call hooks, TypeScript SDK sample that demonstrates structured output + tool invocation, documentation pages in docs/rag/visual-workbench.md, and a short video/screenshot asset. The workbench emphasizes discoverability and repeatability: built-in prompt presets, a small set of example retrievers (memory, simple vector store backed by in-memory embeddings), and test prompts for regression checks.

Highlights: - Visual editor with nodes for retriever, prompt template, LLM, and tool. Nodes expose minimal config properties; the editor serializes to a JSON flow spec compatible with the TypeScript SDK runner. - TypeScript SDK example (packages/sdk-typescript/examples/visual-workbench.ts) showing how to load a flow spec, run a session against hosted or local runtime, and handle function/tool calls with typed inputs/outputs. - Local shim (examples/visual-rag-workbench/shim) that can be started with npm run dev and optionally points at Redwood hosted endpoints via env vars. The shim supports streaming and simulated latency to test UX under different SLOs. - Docs page with step-by-step quickstart, troubleshooting, and guidance on moving from prototype to a Dedicated deployment.

Checklist (what I changed and why): - New example project: examples/visual-rag-workbench (frontend + shim + sample data) - TypeScript SDK sample: packages/sdk-typescript/examples/visual-workbench.ts - Documentation: docs/rag/visual-workbench.md - Static assets: site/static/img/visual-workbench.png, site/static/video/visual-workbench-demo.mp4 (trimmed) - CI: added a playground workflow that boots the shim and runs smoke tests against the example (ci/workflows/playground-visual-workbench.yml) - Tests: integration smoke tests under examples/visual-rag-workbench/test/smoke that validate the flow serialization, tool call stub, and streaming token handling.

Compatibility & security notes: The shim intentionally runs in unprivileged mode and never persists customer secrets. Examples default to a sandboxed in-memory vector store. We added a doc subsection on how to swap the shim to call Redwood hosted endpoints with saved credentials (do not check in). The work intentionally does not change any runtime or production code paths.

How to try locally: 1) cd examples/visual-rag-workbench/frontend && npm install && npm run dev 2) cd ../shim && npm install && REDWOOD_API_KEY=... npm run dev 3) Open http://localhost:3000 and select the local runtime in the top-right. A set of sample flows and prompt presets are available. The README contains a one-line command to seed the sample index.

Testing & CI: The PR includes a lightweight CI job that launches the shim in a container, runs the smoke suite, and verifies the TypeScript example can run against the local endpoint. CI occasionally timed out on the first run due to test port collisions; I added a random port fallback and reran.

Related: ENG-4987 (prototype funding), DES-872 (UX validation), PM-324 (roadmap item for quickstarts).

Open questions / follow-ups: - Consider adding a small WASM-based on-device LLM shim for offline demos (future PR). - Add e2e tests that run the frontend in headless Chrome to validate UX flows.

Merge notes: opted to squash the feature branch into main to preserve a single example commit and simplify bisects.

Author contact: Eleanor Chen (frontend & examples owner).
